title: A Postcards for the Radiators
premise: Ansel Fairweather, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste years ago and has hidden it from everyone, returns to his family's crumbling seaside house for his mother's funeral. There, a stranger addresses the family by 'the Verrones'—a name Ansel has never heard—revealing that his mother lived an entire second identity in the town where she grew up. As the house sale deadline looms, Ansel and his estranged sister Delia uncover letters, a suppressed inheritance, and the truth that their mother's reinvention was built on a betrayal of her own sister, who still lives nearby. In the end, Ansel chooses truth over the family's careful invisibility: he publicly confesses his lost taste, renames himself with the Verrone name in the funeral notice correction, and gives the house to his aunt's care rather than selling it.
about_author: Petra Quintana is a former food writer from coastal Maine who spent a decade reviewing restaurants before turning to fiction about families and the things they refuse to say. Her work has appeared in small literary journals, and this is her first novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At his mother's funeral, Ansel mentally catalogs everything unsaid between them, including his secret loss of taste. He performs grief flawlessly. Emotional beat: hollow competence masking dread.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A stranger at the reception calls the family 'the Verrones.' No one corrects him; no one seems to know why. Ansel pockets the man's card. Beat: first crack in the family's polished surface.

chapters.title: Delia Arrives Late
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Ansel's sister sweeps in from Chicago, all efficiency and estate-sale spreadsheets, eager to close the house fast. Her briskness hides resentment over years of being the one who called, who visited, who was refused. Beat: friction established.

chapters.title: The House That Kept Score
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Sifting through the house, they find a locked writing desk and postcards addressed to 'R. Verrone,' never sent, spanning forty years. Beat: curiosity sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: Tasting Notes
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Back in the city, Ansel files another glowing review he cannot verify, terrified a young editor's questions will expose him. Flashback to the illness that took his taste. Beat: shame deepening.

chapters.title: The Man at the Funeral
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel tracks down the stranger, Tomas, who assumed they were Verrones because their mother, Ruth, visited the town every year under that name. He mentions 'her sister.' Beat: the second life becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: What Delia Knew
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia admits Mother once mentioned a sister, Marion, decades ago, then forbade the subject. Delia chose loyalty to silence over truth. Beat: guilt and complicity revealed.

chapters.title: Return to Salt Hollow
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The siblings drive to the coastal town of Salt Hollow together, bickering, the unsold house behind them and a deadline ahead. Beat: reluctant alliance formed.

chapters.title: Marion's Doorstep
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. They find Marion Verrone, ninety-one, sharp-tongued, living above a shuttered chowder house. She looks at Ansel and says, 'You have her chin before she changed it.' Beat: recognition, hostility, door half-opened.

chapters.title: The Postcards Explained
chapters.summary: Marion's POV. Marion reveals Ruth left after betraying her: Ruth sold Marion's share of the family restaurant to pay a debt, then vanished into a new name and marriage. The postcards were Ruth's annual cowardly apology. Beat: sympathy complicated by anger.

chapters.title: The Deed in the Desk
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Back home, they force the desk and find the original deed showing the restaurant was jointly owned—and a letter naming Ansel's father as complicit. Beat: the betrayal widens across generations.

chapters.title: Review, Revoked
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A food blogger accuses Ansel of fabricating reviews. His editor demands proof. Ansel stalls, lying more elaborately than ever. Beat: professional world beginning to collapse in parallel with the family one.

chapters.title: Delia's Ledger
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia confronts what her own silences cost—a marriage ended by secrets she kept for Mother. She decides the sale must wait. Beat: Delia flips from closer to holdout.

chapters.title: The Buyer's Deadline
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The developer buying the house threatens legal action as the closing date nears. Delia stalls; Ansel wavers, tempted to let it all be paved over. Beat: external pressure mounting.

chapters.title: Chowder, Unsweetened
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Marion cooks for him from the old Verrone recipes. Ansel confesses he cannot taste it. Instead of pity, she says, 'Then you'll finally have to take someone's word.' Beat: intimacy through honesty; Ansel's secret surfaces safely for the first time.

chapters.title: The Public Confession
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel publishes a column admitting his anosmia and years of borrowed descriptions, dismantling his career deliberately. Beat: climax of the personal arc—truth chosen over image.

chapters.title: The Funeral Notice Correction
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia runs a corrected obituary listing Ruth Fairweather Verrone, survived by a sister. Their father calls, furious; Delia holds the line. Beat: climax of the loyalty-vs-truth theme.

chapters.title: What Marion Wants
chapters.summary: Marion's POV. Marion admits she never wanted money back—she wanted to be acknowledged before she died. She asks only that the chowder house sign be restored, not the building saved. Beat: expectations subverted; grace offered.

chapters.title: The Closing
chapters.summary: Both POVs. At the sale signing, Ansel and Delia instead transfer the house to a land trust co-held with Marion, scuttling the developer deal at real financial cost. Beat: costly, irreversible choice made.

chapters.title: Fallout
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Consequences land: the lawsuit settles cheaply, their father cuts contact, Ansel loses column but gains a podcast about taste and memory. Beat: losses tallied honestly, not prettily.

chapters.title: First Course
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Months later, Ansel tastes something—faintly, maybe psychosomatically—at Marion's table during the sign restoration. Whether real or imagined, he weeps. Beat: tentative healing.

chapters.title: Postcards, Finally Sent
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The siblings mail Ruth's forty unsent postcards to Marion, one per week, with their own notes added beneath. The last line is Ansel's inventory finally emptied. Beat: resolution—truth delivered late, but delivered.
